items.title: US and Russia reach informal deal as New START treaty expires

featured_image.name: Explainer: Could US and Russia extend last nuclear weapons treaty?

items.description:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres on Wednesday urged the United States and Russia to negotiate a new nuclear arms control framework "without delay" as the New START treaty expired at midnight, warning that the world now faces the highest risk of nuclear weapons use "in decades."[1][2][3]

The expiration of the 2010 agreement—which capped both nations' deployed strategic nuclear warheads at 1,550 and established verification mechanisms—marks what Guterres called "a grave moment for international peace and security." For the first time in more than 50 years, no binding limits exist on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the two nations that together possess roughly 87% of the world's nuclear weapons.[2][4][5][1]

items.title: Xi urges Trump to handle Taiwan arms sales 'with prudence'

featured_image.name: China's Xi reasserts Taiwan stance in call with Trump, while U.S. ...

items.description: Chinese President Xi Jinping urged President Donald Trump to handle arms sales to Taiwan "with prudence" during a phone call on Wednesday, February 4, underscoring Beijing's view that the Taiwan issue remains "the most important issue" in U.S.-China relations. The exchange, the first direct conversation between the two leaders since November, came as both sides prepared for Trump's planned April visit to Beijing.[1][2]

items.title: Wargame finds Russia could seize Lithuanian city in days

featured_image.name: Wargame simulates how Russia could take Nato country 'within days'

items.description: A tabletop military exercise conducted by former German and NATO officials in December 2025 concluded that Russia could capture the strategically vital Lithuanian city of Marijampole within days by exploiting allied indecision rather than overwhelming force. The findings, published this week, have intensified scrutiny of NATO's decision-making capabilities and political resolve in a potential crisis.

items.title: US and China accelerate 'messy divorce' across critical sectors

featured_image.name: US-China decoupling is crossing a Rubicon | Reuters

items.description:
The United States and China are methodically untangling their economic relationship across critical sectors including semiconductors, food, and energy, marking what The Wall Street Journal calls a "messy divorce" between the world's two largest economies.[1][2][3]

China has committed an estimated $1 trillion since early 2024 toward achieving economic self-sufficiency, with funds flowing to soybean farmers in the northeastern grain belt, semiconductor manufacturers seeking to break reliance on Western technology, and renewable energy infrastructure, according to the Journal's analysis by Lingling Wei and Jeanne Whalen.[2][3]

items.title: Russian forces lose Starlink access, halting assaults in Ukraine

featured_image.name: Ukraine destroying Musk's Starlink systems being used by Russia

items.description:
Starlink terminals used by Russian military units went dark on Wednesday across the entire front line in Ukraine, causing what one Ukrainian official described as a "catastrophe" for Russian forces and halting assault operations in multiple sectors.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, adviser to Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on technological issues, said the loss of satellite connectivity has crippled Russian coordination. "For the enemy at the front, this is not just a problem — it's a catastrophe. Command and control have completely collapsed. Assault operations have been halted in many areas," Beskrestnov told Ukrainska Pravda on Thursday.[1][2]

Russian military bloggers confirmed the outages, reporting that no amount of terminal reboots would restore the connection. One pro-Kremlin channel noted the situation "has effectively reverted to February 2022, when there was a complete lack of coordination between Russian units".[2][3]

items.title: Last US-Russia nuclear arms treaty expires, ending decades of limits

featured_image.name: UN chief calls New START expiration 'grave moment' | Reuters

items.description:
The New START treaty officially expired at midnight GMT on Thursday, marking the first time in more than half a century that the United States and Russia operate without legally binding constraints on their strategic nuclear arsenals. UN Secretary-General António Guterres issued a stark warning, urging both nations to return to the negotiating table "without delay."

"The expiration of the New START Treaty marks a grave moment for international peace and security," Guterres said in a statement released as the treaty lapsed. "For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the Russian Federation and the United States of America, the two States that possess the overwhelming majority of the global stockpile of nuclear weapons."[1][2]

items.title: India to sign trade deal with US in March, minister says

featured_image.name: Piyush Goyal meets US commerce secretary for 2nd time in a ...

items.description:
India and the United States are set to finalize a formal trade agreement in March that will dramatically slash tariffs and reshape commercial ties between the world's two largest democracies, Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal announced Thursday.

The long-awaited deal, first unveiled by President Donald Trump on February 2, will cut U.S. duties on Indian exports to 18% from the current 50%, while India commits to eliminating tariffs on American industrial goods and purchasing over $500 billion worth of U.S. products over five years.[1][2][3]

items.title: European stocks flat as ECB, Bank of England set to hold rates

featured_image.name: Rising Euro, Falling Inflation In Focus At ECB Meeting

items.description:
European equities traded flat on Thursday as investors weighed a mixed bag of earnings reports and braced for monetary policy decisions from two major central banks scheduled later in the day.

The pan-European STOXX 600 held steady at around 618 points in early trading, hovering near the record high reached the previous session. Meanwhile, Germany's DAX and France's CAC 40 showed minimal movement as the market awaited clarity from the European Central Bank and Bank of England.[1]

items.title: OpenAI hiring hundreds of consultants to expand enterprise AI

featured_image.name: OpenAI offers custom AI consulting services to clients at ...

items.description:
OpenAI is significantly accelerating its enterprise ambitions by recruiting hundreds of technical consultants who will embed directly with large corporate clients to build custom AI solutions, according to a report by The Information. The hiring push reflects the company's shift from pure technology provider to full-service enterprise partner as it competes for high-value business contracts.[1][2]

The ChatGPT maker is expanding its team of "forward-deployed engineers" who work directly with organizations to adapt models to proprietary data and build custom applications, including AI agents capable of automating employee tasks. The company currently employs roughly 60 such engineers along with 200 customer success staff, making this expansion a major rebalancing of its workforce toward enterprise implementation.[3][4][5][1]

items.title: Nasdaq posts worst two-day drop since October amid AI fears

featured_image.name: Google parent Alphabet predicts a sharp surge in 2026 capital spending on AI

items.description:
A two-day rout in technology shares deepened Thursday as investors in Asia and Europe continued to flee the sector, spooked by fears over ballooning artificial intelligence investment costs and growing concerns that AI tools could disrupt the software industry.

The Nasdaq Composite recorded its worst two-day decline since October, breaching its 100-day moving average as selling extended from software makers into semiconductor stocks and other companies tied to AI infrastructure development. In Asia, the MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled 1.8%, weighed down by a 3.9% plunge in South Korea's Kospi and a 1.5% drop in Taiwan's Taiex.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Volvo Cars Q4 profit tumbles 68% amid tariffs and weak demand

featured_image.name: Sweden's Volvo Cars switches gears in the U.S. as tariffs bite

items.description: Volvo Cars reported a sharp decline in fourth-quarter profits on Thursday, blaming U.S. tariffs, weak consumer demand, and the removal of electric vehicle incentives for its struggles. Meanwhile, Toyota Motor Corporation is expected to report its third consecutive quarterly profit drop when it releases results this week, as rising costs and trade levies continue to pressure the world's largest automaker.

items.title: Asian markets tumble as global tech selloff enters third day

featured_image.name: Kospi dips nearly 2% as AI bubble worries resurface

items.description: Technology stocks extended a punishing selloff on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq Composite declining 1.5 percent for its worst two-day drop since last April's tariff-fueled turmoil. The global rout deepened as Asian markets followed Wall Street lower amid mounting concerns about artificial intelligence disruption and frothy valuations.

items.title: UN chief calls New START expiration a 'grave moment'

featured_image.name: UN chief calls New START expiration 'grave moment' - Reuters

items.description:
The New START treaty, the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement between the United States and Russia, expired at midnight GMT on Thursday, February 5, leaving the world without binding limits on the two largest nuclear arsenals for the first time in more than half a century.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the expiration "a grave moment for international peace and security" and urged both nations to return to the negotiating table without delay.[1][2][3][4][5]

"For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the Russian Federation and the United States of America—the two States that possess the overwhelming majority of the global stockpile of nuclear weapons," Guterres said in a statement released Wednesday.[2][3][1]

items.title: Gold tops $5,000 as weak jobs data fuels rate-cut hopes

featured_image.name: Gold's record run rolls on with prices surging past $US5,000 ...

items.description:
Gold reclaimed the key $5,000 level on Wednesday, climbing more than 1% to around $5,017 per ounce as safe-haven demand intensified amid rising geopolitical tensions and fresh signs of labor market softness in the United States. The rally marks a rebound for the precious metal after a volatile stretch that saw prices swing from a record high of nearly $5,595 late last month to a sharp plunge below $4,400 just days ago.

The surge comes as U.S. and Iranian officials confirmed high-stakes nuclear talks will take place Friday in Oman, with considerable uncertainty over whether the two sides can bridge wide gaps on Iran's nuclear program, ballistic missiles, and regional activities. Silver followed suit, jumping nearly 10% to around $91 per ounce.[1][2][3]

items.title: Oil prices dip as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman

featured_image.name: US-Iran nuclear talks set for Oman on Friday, Tehran confirms

items.description:
Global oil prices fell on Wednesday evening as Washington and Tehran confirmed they would hold direct negotiations in Oman on Friday, easing fears of imminent conflict between the two nations.

U.S. crude slipped by about 1% to $64.50 per barrel in Asian trading late Wednesday, while Brent fell to approximately $68.49 per barrel, according to Reuters. The decline marked oil's first retreat in three days, following a 4.8% surge in the previous two sessions driven by fears of potential military strikes against the OPEC producer.[1][2][3]

items.title: Oil prices fall as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman

featured_image.name: Trump-Iran latest: US military shoots down Iranian drone as Tehran demands venue change for talks

items.description:
Crude oil prices have swung sharply this week as military confrontations between the United States and Iran collided with diplomatic efforts, with markets reacting first to the collapse and then the revival of nuclear negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

West Texas Intermediate crude fell more than 1% on Thursday after the U.S. and Iran confirmed they will meet in Oman on Friday to discuss Iran's nuclear program, easing fears that recent hostilities could spiral into open conflict. The decline followed a roughly 3% surge the previous day, when the talks appeared on the verge of falling apart.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Engineers propose 50-mile seabed curtain to slow Thwaites melt

featured_image.name: This 'Doomsday Glacier' is melting faster than anyone thought. Now Earth's biggest cities are in danger

items.description:
A consortium of researchers and engineers is proposing to construct an 80-kilometer underwater barrier to shield Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier from the warm ocean currents driving its rapid deterioration. The ambitious Seabed Curtain Project comes as new data gathered from beneath the glacier reveals turbulent, warm waters capable of accelerating ice loss at an alarming rate.

The proposed structure would stand approximately 150 meters high and be anchored to the seabed at a depth of around 650 meters, forming a physical barrier to restrict the influx of warm water that is melting the glacier from below. The project aims to complete deployment by 2040, with an estimated construction cost of $40 to $80 billion and annual maintenance of $1 to $2 billion over its projected 25-year lifespan.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Last U.S.-Russia nuclear arms treaty set to expire Wednesday

featured_image.name: Last Russia-US treaty on nuclear arms control set to expire

items.description:
For the first time in over fifty years, the world's two largest nuclear powers will operate without limitations on their arsenals after the New START treaty expires on February 5, 2026. The lapse of the agreement, signed in 2010, marks the end of decades of arms control diplomacy between Washington and Moscow and raises concerns about a new era of nuclear competition that could also involve China.

The treaty, which capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550 and delivery systems at 700 for each nation, also required on-site inspections and data exchanges—measures that had been suspended since Russia halted its participation following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.[1][2][3]

items.title: Oil surges as U.S.-Iran talks revived after near collapse

featured_image.name: Oil falls on U.S.-Iran de-escalation, easing supply worries

items.description: Oil prices jumped nearly 3 percent on Wednesday after nuclear talks between the United States and Iran briefly collapsed, before being revived following intense lobbying by Arab allies. The market swings underscored the fragility of diplomatic efforts to defuse tensions between Washington and Tehran amid a significant U.S. military buildup in the Middle East.

items.title: Heavy snowfall cancels training as 2026 Winter Olympics open

featured_image.name: Heavy snowfall prompts cancellation of women’s downhill training at Milan Cortina Olympics

items.description:
As the Milan-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics prepare for their February 6 opening ceremony, organizers face a climate change paradox: decades of warming have left venues dependent on artificial snow, yet an intense last-minute snowfall has now forced the cancellation of training runs.

The 2026 Games are taking place in a much warmer climate than when Cortina d'Ampezzo last hosted in 1956, highlighting the growing challenge of staging winter sports in an era of rising global temperatures.
